purpose: Auto-generated held-out decision benchmark (decision-bench-gen.py). Grounded in the brain's own corpus; spot-check before trusting fleet numbers.

cases.situation: You are evaluating a major investment in a large, complex financial institution. You recognize going in that the business is unusually complicated, carries significant regulatory and reputational danger, and could require heavy hands-on involvement if things go wrong. The headline valuation still looks reasonably cheap. Do you proceed with the investment anyway, or walk away because of the inherent danger and complexity?
options: Proceed with the investment because the price is attractive enough to justify the risk
Walk away entirely, refusing to enter a situation you know is too dangerous and too much trouble
Take a small token position to monitor the situation without real exposure
cases.actual_decision: Proceeded with the investment (Salomon Brothers) despite recognizing upfront that it was too dangerous and too much trouble.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger later admitted the investment caused prolonged agony and required crisis intervention to avoid collapse, concluding afterward that the right answer to 'too much trouble, too much danger' is simply not to enter, regardless of price.
cases.source: Hard lesson: Salomon Brothers mistake quote

cases.situation: For two to three decades your investment strategy has been to buy mediocre, cheap businesses at bargain prices and hold them for value realization, an approach that has been reliably profitable. However, you increasingly sense the approach caps your long-term returns and requires unpleasant workouts. Do you continue with the proven cheap-but-mediocre strategy since it is 'coining money,' or abandon it entirely for a fundamentally different approach of paying fair prices for great businesses?
options: Continue the cigar-butt strategy since it demonstrably works and is profitable
Abandon the cigar-butt approach entirely and shift to buying wonderful businesses at fair prices
Blend both strategies, keeping cigar-butts as a smaller allocation alongside quality names
cases.actual_decision: Abandoned the cigar-butt strategy entirely in favor of buying wonderful businesses at fair prices.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger recognized the cigar-butt approach could not scale and was 'kind of scrunchy,' and used the See's Candies insight to persuade Buffett to shift Berkshire's entire philosophy toward quality compounders.
cases.source: Hard lesson: 20-30 years buying bad businesses cheap

cases.situation: You have decided to build a full 100-million-share position in a retailer you believe is a great, mispriced opportunity, and you begin buying at around $23 a share. Shortly after your initial purchase, the stock price ticks up modestly. Do you continue buying aggressively at the slightly higher price to complete your intended position, or hold off and wait for the price to come back down to your original entry point?
options: Pay up and continue buying at the slightly higher price to complete the full intended position
Wait for the stock to retrace to the original entry price before buying more
Abandon the additional purchases and keep only the small initial position
cases.actual_decision: Waited for the stock to come back down instead of paying the slightly higher price, and never completed the intended position.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger later admitted this was pure anchoring to the initial entry price — 'thumb-sucking' hesitation rather than genuine caution — and estimated it cost Berkshire roughly $10 billion in foregone gains.
cases.source: Hard lesson: Walmart ~$10 billion mistake

cases.situation: Warren Buffett, your longtime investing partner, has been trained by Ben Graham to buy only statistically cheap, mediocre businesses. A high-quality candy company is available, but only at a price well above the traditional cigar-butt bargain level. Do you advise sticking with the cheap-business discipline that has worked for years, or push hard to pay a real premium for a genuinely great business?
options: Advise passing on the deal since the price is too high relative to Graham-style bargains
Push Buffett to pay the premium price because the business quality justifies it
Suggest a smaller, token position to test the thesis without committing full capital
cases.actual_decision: Pushed Buffett to pay a real premium for See's Candies, a genuinely great business.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger viewed this as the pivotal insight that reoriented Berkshire's entire philosophy from cigar-butt bargains to durable, high-quality compounders — a single correct insight that changed everything.
cases.source: Biography 1972: See's Candies acquisition

cases.situation: You are hired as legal counsel to advise a client on a promising real estate development project. In the course of advising, you identify what looks like a highly attractive opportunity. Do you stay strictly in your role as advisor and simply collect your legal fee, or step across the line and put your own capital in as a co-investor alongside your client?
options: Remain purely as legal advisor and collect the standard fee, avoiding any conflict of interest
Cross the line and become a co-investor, putting personal capital into the deal alongside the client
Recommend the opportunity to other investors instead of participating personally
cases.actual_decision: Crossed the line from advisor to principal, putting his own money in and owning half of the operation.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger deliberately chose to risk his own capital alongside his client rather than merely collecting a fee, and the project (Caltech real estate) sold out quickly.
cases.source: Documented choice: Caltech real estate co-investment

cases.situation: You hold a senior leadership position at a major conglomerate. Opportunities arise to take on chairmanship of a separate financial company, chair a legacy print/media business, and sit on the board of a large retailer, all simultaneously with your main role. Do you decline the additional roles to focus fully on your primary position, or take on all of them at once?
options: Decline the additional roles and concentrate solely on the primary leadership position
Accept all roles simultaneously, spreading attention across multiple institutions
Accept only one additional role to limit dilution of focus
cases.actual_decision: Took on all the additional roles simultaneously — Vice Chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, Chairman of Wesco Financial, Chairman of Daily Journal Corporation, and Director of Costco.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger valued active engagement across diverse institutions as a source of continued learning and contribution rather than narrowing his focus.
cases.source: Documented choice: multiple leadership roles

cases.situation: You are in your late 90s, having spent decades on corporate boards. Your peers of similar age have long since retired from active director duties. Do you step back from board service to enjoy a quiet retirement, or continue actively serving on multiple corporate boards well into your late 90s?
options: Retire from all board positions to focus on personal life and legacy
Continue serving actively on multiple boards well into your late 90s
Retain one board seat as an honorary, largely ceremonial role
cases.actual_decision: Continued serving actively on multiple boards — Berkshire Hathaway, Daily Journal, and Costco — well into his late 90s.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger believed in active contribution over passive retirement, maintaining the habits of mind that had made him effective throughout his life until the very end.
cases.source: Documented choice: board service into late 90s

cases.situation: As an advisor to a friend and business partner who has built his early success on the classic Ben Graham method of buying statistically cheap, mediocre companies, you must decide what strategic advice to give him about the future direction of his growing capital base. Do you tell him to keep replicating the model that built his fortune, or urge him to abandon it altogether?
options: Advise him to keep buying more companies like his original vehicle, since the formula has worked
Advise him to stop buying more of the same and instead add wonderful businesses at fair prices
Advise a mixed approach, keeping some cigar-butt purchases while testing quality names
cases.actual_decision: Advised abandoning the cigar-butt approach entirely and instead adding wonderful businesses purchased at fair prices.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger told Buffett to 'forget about ever buying another company like Berkshire' and instead focus on wonderful businesses at fair prices, giving up fair businesses at wonderful prices — a reorientation that reshaped Berkshire's whole philosophy.
leak_markers: Forget about ever buying another company like Berkshire
cases.source: Documented choice: 1965 advice to Buffett

cases.situation: You have co-founded a law firm and built a promising, prestigious legal career after graduating from Harvard Law School. At the same time, you are increasingly drawn to investing and have begun a partnership with a talented investor friend. Do you continue building your legal career at the firm you helped found, or leave law practice early to pivot fully into investing?
options: Continue building the legal career at the firm, treating investing as a side interest
Leave active law practice after just a few years to pivot entirely into investing
Split time evenly between law practice and investing indefinitely
cases.actual_decision: Left active law practice after only three years at the firm he co-founded, pivoting entirely to investing with Warren Buffett.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger was willing to abandon a prestigious legal career at the height of his potential because he saw investing with Buffett as the better path.
cases.source: Documented choice: left law practice for investing

cases.situation: You have accumulated significant wealth and want to give a large sum to philanthropy. You could spread your giving broadly across many causes and institutions to maximize reach, or concentrate it heavily on a small number of institutions you understand deeply and personally care about, such as a university law school. Which approach do you take?
options: Spread philanthropic giving broadly across many different causes and institutions
Concentrate giving heavily on a small number of institutions you understand and care about deeply, such as law schools
Set up a broad-based foundation to distribute funds according to need rather than personal preference
cases.actual_decision: Concentrated giving heavily on institutions he understood and cared about deeply, particularly universities and legal education — including a $43.5 million gift to Stanford Law School's dormitories.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger preferred deep, informed philanthropy over broad, diffuse giving, applying the same focus he used in investing to his charitable decisions.
cases.source: Documented choice: philanthropic concentration

cases.situation: You have accumulated billions of dollars over your career, and your closest business partner has chosen to direct the overwhelming majority of his fortune to public foundations rather than to his own family. You must decide how to allocate your own wealth between your descendants and philanthropic foundations.
options: Follow your partner's approach and direct the large majority of wealth to public foundations
Distribute more than half of your wealth directly to your descendants
Split wealth roughly evenly between descendants and foundations
cases.actual_decision: Distributed more than half of his wealth to his descendants rather than to public foundations.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger made a deliberately different capital allocation decision than Buffett, viewing it as a conscious choice reflecting his own values about family and legacy.
cases.source: Documented choice: wealth distribution to descendants

cases.situation: A competitor launches a direct attack on your candy business by opening copycat stores designed to confuse and siphon customers from your brand. Do you take a measured, wait-and-see approach to see if the copycat effort fizzles on its own, or respond immediately and aggressively with legal force?
options: Wait and monitor the situation before deciding whether legal action is warranted
Respond immediately and aggressively with legal action against the copycat stores
Ignore the competitor and focus resources on strengthening your own brand instead
cases.actual_decision: Responded immediately and aggressively with legal force against the copycat 'Mrs. Stover's' stores.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger's operating principle was to attack problems instantly and decisively, believing prevention is worth a ton of cure.
leak_markers: prevention is worth a ton of cure
cases.source: Documented choice: Russell Stover / See's Candies defense

cases.situation: A prominent tech executive is being pressured by a tabloid publication with material he considers extortion. He chooses to publicly name the publication and resist rather than quietly pay or ignore the threat. As an observer and fellow business leader, do you criticize this public confrontation as reckless and reputation-damaging, or view it as admirable behavior regardless of political fallout?
options: Criticize the public confrontation as unnecessarily risky and reputation-damaging
View the confrontation as exemplary, admirable behavior regardless of the fallout
Take a neutral stance, declining to comment on another executive's personal conflict
cases.actual_decision: Viewed the public confrontation as exemplary behavior, admiring the willingness to confront the problem head-on.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger admired people who confront problems head-on and had 'no quarrel' with the decision, regarding the tabloid as a 'little nothing place.'
cases.source: Documented choice: admiration for Bezos confronting Enquirer

cases.situation: You've identified a globally dominant beverage company whose stock you believe is significantly mispriced relative to its true quality. Do you accumulate the position gradually and discreetly over a long period to avoid moving the market and to preserve optionality, or buy as aggressively as possible, even representing a large fraction of daily trading volume, for months on end?
options: Accumulate the position slowly and discreetly to avoid drawing attention or moving the price
Buy as aggressively as possible, representing roughly a third of daily trading volume, sustained over months
Wait for a market downturn to buy the full position at a single depressed price point
cases.actual_decision: Bought as aggressively as possible, representing roughly one-third of total daily trading volume every day for months.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger believed true conviction in a mispriced great business warrants aggressive, concentrated, sustained buying rather than caution.
cases.source: Documented choice: Coca-Cola aggressive buying

cases.situation: You are helping select new investment managers to join the firm's capital allocation team. Candidates come with strong track records and impressive credentials, but you also personally value voracious, wide-ranging reading as core to how you and your partner think. Do you prioritize traditional investment credentials and track record, or specifically select candidates because they read as intensely as you and your partner do?
options: Select managers primarily based on investment track record and credentials
Select managers specifically because they read as voraciously as you and your partner do
Select managers based on a formal test of financial modeling skill
cases.actual_decision: Selected the two managers specifically because they read as voraciously as Buffett and Munger did.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger described himself as 'a book with legs' and believed the depth and breadth gained from constant reading was the defining trait to look for in future capital allocators.
leak_markers: read as much as we did
cases.source: Documented choice: hiring Weschler/Combs for reading habits

cases.situation: Your firm has accumulated a large cash position because no sufficiently attractive investment opportunities currently exist. Analysts and shareholders are pressuring you to deploy the capital into something — anything — rather than let it sit idle earning minimal returns. Do you force deployment into mediocre opportunities to put the cash to work, or let the cash continue to build up until a genuinely intelligent opportunity appears?
options: Deploy the cash into available but mediocre opportunities rather than let it sit idle
Let the cash build up indefinitely until a genuinely intelligent opportunity appears
Return the excess cash to shareholders via buybacks or dividends rather than hold it
cases.actual_decision: Let the cash build up rather than deploying it into suboptimal opportunities.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger considered it entirely rational to do nothing when nothing intelligent presented itself, famously asking 'what the hell is wrong with that?'
leak_markers: what the hell is wrong with that
cases.source: Documented choice: holding cash rationally

cases.situation: You and your business partner are building an investment operation that will eventually manage enormous sums of capital. Nearly all major financial institutions are headquartered in New York or other big financial centers, where you'd have direct access to Wall Street networks, deal flow, and talent. Do you locate your operation in a major financial hub, or deliberately base it in a quiet Midwestern city far from that environment?
options: Locate the operation in New York or another major financial hub for access to networks and deal flow
Deliberately base the operation in a quiet Midwestern city away from financial-center social pressure
Split operations between a financial hub and a secondary base
cases.actual_decision: Deliberately chose Omaha rather than New York or Los Angeles.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger and Buffett believed the environment in Omaha did not apply the same social pressure that a major financial center would, producing clarity for independent thinking.
cases.source: Documented choice: choosing Omaha deliberately

cases.situation: You are evaluating what kind of business model to build or endorse. One path involves selling products that customers genuinely benefit from, even if that limits certain profit-maximizing tactics. Another path involves selling products or services that exploit psychological weaknesses or trick customers, which could be more profitable in the short run. Which approach do you personally favor, even at the cost of potentially lower profits?
options: Favor selling products that are genuinely good for customers, even if it means less profit
Favor whichever approach maximizes profit, including tactics that exploit customer psychology
Favor a hybrid approach that maximizes profit while avoiding only the most egregious tricks
cases.actual_decision: Favored selling things that are genuinely good for people, even at the cost of making less money.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger believed this approach, exemplified by Costco, produces superior long-term business results in addition to being more ethical.
leak_markers: instead of stuff that tricks them
cases.source: Documented choice: preference for honest business models

cases.situation: A high-profile joint healthcare venture backed by several major companies and led by well-known executives ultimately fails to achieve its ambitious goals and is shut down. As an outside observer and industry commentator, do you dismiss the venture as a wasteful failure with no redeeming value, or credit it with providing value despite its failure?
options: Dismiss the venture as a wasteful failure with no lasting value
Credit the venture as a valuable 'constructive disruptor' despite its ultimate failure
Withhold judgment, considering it too early to assess the venture's impact
cases.actual_decision: Credited the venture as valuable, calling its leaders 'constructive disruptors' despite the failure.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger believed even failed disruptors provide value by forcing incumbents to examine and defend their business models, as a competitor's CEO himself acknowledged.
cases.source: Documented choice: view on Haven healthcare venture

cases.situation: You've identified an investment you are absolutely certain will succeed, based on deep research and conviction. Sizing decisions matter enormously to long-term outcomes. Do you allow this single high-conviction position to grow to whatever size your certainty justifies, potentially the majority of your net worth, or do you cap it at a fixed maximum regardless of how confident you feel?
options: Allow the position to grow as large as conviction justifies, even beyond half of net worth
Cap any single investment at a fixed maximum, such as 25% of net worth, regardless of conviction
Set no formal cap but review position size annually based on changing circumstances
cases.actual_decision: Capped any single investment at a maximum of 25% of net worth, regardless of certainty level.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger believed that because being wrong about any single bet is always possible, a fixed cap ensures a painful but survivable loss rather than total financial ruin.
cases.source: Documented choice: 25% position cap rule

cases.situation: You are building wealth early in your career and every dollar not invested is a dollar not compounding. Financial optimizers argue that holding idle cash is inefficient and that all available capital should be deployed for maximum growth. Do you keep a substantial cash cushion set aside at all times, even while young and actively building wealth, or invest essentially everything to maximize compounding?
options: Invest essentially all available capital to maximize compounding, minimizing idle cash
Maintain a minimum of two years' living expenses in cash at all times, even while building wealth
Keep only a small emergency buffer of a few months' expenses rather than a full two years
cases.actual_decision: Maintained a minimum of two years of living expenses in cash at all times, even when young and building wealth.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger believed this reserve converts emergency situations from immediate catastrophes into manageable problems, eliminating forced decisions during crises.
cases.source: Documented choice: maintaining 2-year cash reserve

cases.situation: Over the course of a decades-long investing career, some industries you once understood deeply have changed so much — new technology, new business models — that your prior expertise may no longer apply. Do you continue asserting the same level of competence you once had in those industries out of professional pride, or openly acknowledge that your circle of competence in those areas has shrunk?
options: Continue asserting the same competence in those industries, relying on past expertise
Openly acknowledge that the boundaries of competence have shifted and admit reduced understanding
Quietly stop commenting on those industries without explicitly admitting reduced competence
cases.actual_decision: Openly acknowledged that the boundaries of his own circle of competence had shifted over time.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger believed intellectual honesty required acknowledging when industries had changed enough that he could no longer claim the same competence he once had.
cases.source: Documented choice: acknowledging shifted competence boundaries

cases.situation: You are assessing whether to engage with complex financial derivative instruments that offer sophisticated hedging and return possibilities, but whose true underlying risks are difficult for even experienced practitioners to fully model. Do you learn the instruments deeply enough to use them selectively for advantage, or stay entirely away from them as a category?
options: Learn the instruments deeply and use them selectively where advantageous
Stay entirely away from derivatives as a category due to their opaque, systemic danger
Use derivatives only in small, tightly hedged positions to limit exposure
cases.actual_decision: Stayed entirely away from derivatives, describing them as weapons of mass financial destruction.
cases.actual_reasoning: Munger believed the complexity of derivative instruments made their true risks invisible to most participants, and his instinct with large dangerous unknowns was to stay far away rather than get close to the line.
cases.source: Documented choice: skepticism and avoidance of derivatives
